en: The Scripture on Realizing the Seal of the Mahāyāna, Volume One; also titled *The Scripture on Entering the Sphere of Wisdom of All Buddhas and the Tathāgatagarbha of Vairocana*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Divākara of India during the Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was at the supreme site atop Mount Malaya.

The gardens were lush and expansive, and the ponds and streams were bright and pure. Great Vidyādharas roamed there, dwelling among the flowers; it was a place inhabited by spirits and not trodden by ordinary men—a realm for attaining the fruits of immortality, supernatural powers, and supreme accomplishment. He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were great śrāvakas who had completed what was to be done—namely, those who had transcended all stages such as those of the *pṛthagjana* and *brāhmaṇa*.
Their leaders were as follows: the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others like them.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by a great assembly of bodhisattvas, all of whom were supreme transcendents. They had all realized and manifested before them the samādhis and dhāraṇīs of all bodhisattvas, possessing mastery and unimpededness, and they dwelt upon all the stages of the bodhisattvas. Their names were:

the noble Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mahamati Bodhisattva, Vijñānamati Bodhisattva, Dṛḍhamati Bodhisattva, Śāntamati Bodhisattva, Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, Anantamati Bodhisattva, Sāgaramati Bodhisattva, Prajñāmati Bodhisattva, Vimalamati Bodhisattva, and Jñānamati Bodhisattva. With these and others as their leaders, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were all recipients of the prediction of enlightenment, each destined to attain perfect awakening in their respective worlds and turn the wheel of Dharma.

Furthermore, various other great devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and rishis—spirits with diverse forms, diverse garments, and diverse head-ornaments, bearing various weapons, various banners, and various standards—all came together to hear the Dharma and sat in the assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly as vast as the ocean, who gazed upon him with reverence and made offerings. He expounded the sublime Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; excellent in meaning and excellent in expression; unique and perfect; fully revealing the pure and holy life.
At that time, in the great city of Laṅkā, there was a rākṣasa king named Vibhīṣaṇa who served as its ruler.

Then Vibhīṣaṇa heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was at the sublime site on the peak of Mount Malaya—a place frequented by sages, filled with great gardens and ponds, a realm of supreme accomplishment inaccessible to ordinary men—where he was surrounded by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as various bodhisattvas and devas, expounding the wondrous Dharma and revealing the pure and stainless holy life.
Thereupon, the householder Vimala had this thought: "The voice of the Buddha is as difficult to hear as the udumbara flower;
how much more so to encounter the appearance of a Buddha and listen to and receive the True Dharma? This is as exceedingly rare as a blind sea turtle encountering the hole of a floating log."

A Buddha is extremely difficult to encounter; the True Dharma is difficult to hear. To hear the Dharma and realize the Path, to behold the World-Honored Buddha, to attain Great Bodhi, and to awaken sentient beings—this is most difficult, most difficult; it is rare indeed to meet such an occasion.

Now that I have encountered this rare opportunity to meet [the Buddha], I should quickly prepare and bring various precious jewels, pearls, necklaces, and immeasurable flower garlands; I should offer incense for burning, smearing, and powdering, as well as robes, parasols, banners, canopies, and curtains, along with flutes, drums, and other musical instruments, and various performers to provide all manner of offerings.

Together with their retinues, they went to the place where the Buddha was, made offerings to him, and inquired about the True Dharma; thus their lives were not lived in vain, and they obtained great benefit within this very body.
At that time, Vipaśyin universally addressed his followers:

"You should all quickly bring forth abundant wealth and treasures—gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, ruby, jade, and pearl necklaces and garlands; as well as exquisite flowers and incense, even including flutes, drums, and various musical instruments, along with entertainers and diverse offerings."

Let us all quickly prepare ourselves and go together to the presence of the Tathāgata, the Lord of Dharma, the Victorious One of the Three Realms, the Supreme Accumulation of Merit, who possesses the most excellent marks, all-knowing vision, and is the supreme field of merit for all-encompassing wisdom, so that we may personally perform offerings to him.
Why is this? The appearance of a Buddha is extremely rare; he manifests but once in a great while. To encounter such a time of merit is a chance met but rarely in an instant.
The sound of the Triple Gem is difficult to hear in this world; this opportunity must not be lost.
The householder Vimala addressed him with these verses:
“Only at times does a Buddha appear in the world; An encounter in a single kṣaṇa is exceedingly difficult.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, It is rare indeed to meet with such a one!”
A Teacher is difficult to encounter, Like the udumbara flower;
The boundless realms of sentient beings Revolve through the six destinies.
In the hells they suffer bitter poisons, As do those in the animal and hungry ghost realms.
Born amidst the eight difficulties, they abandon all Tathāgatas;
yet the Holy Light appears in the world, universally benefiting all sentient beings;
with the sun of great wisdom, it illuminates and extinguishes the darkness of ignorance.
Now we shall go together to him, to perform a great offering for the Honored One, the Mahānāga, the Guide of all the world,
the Great Teacher of gods and humans!
"By making offerings, one obtains great fruit.

When Vimalaprabhā had spoken this verse, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light issued forth from the Buddha; they blazed through the air and entered the great city of Laṅkā, illuminating Vimalaprabhā and her retinue.
When Vīravikrāmin and the others encountered this radiance, they leaped for joy with great delight.
From within the great web of light, sublime verses emerged, expounding the most profound Dharma:
"All phenomena are fundamentally quiescent; Their nature is emptiness and selflessness."
All sentient beings are ultimately ungraspable;
they have no beginning, no middle, and likewise no end.
They are false and unreal, just like illusions and dreams.
Like clouds, like lightning, like a mirage, like floating bubbles;
like a whirling firebrand, like a mass of foam on water—
all phenomena born of causes and conditions are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Know that all conditioned phenomena are exactly like this!
Ignorance and craving are the root of birth and death;
through diligent cultivation of contemplation, ignorance and craving will cease to exist.
"All dharmas are free from verbal expression;
their most ultimate and pure nature is like empty space.

After these verses were proclaimed within the sound of the *Jālinīprabha*, the Lord of Wealth, Vibhīṣaṇa, immediately attained the profound *dharmanidhyānakṣānti* of non-self. Among his remaining followers, some attained the *kṣānti*, some gave rise to the bodhicitta, some attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti*, and some realized the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Viviṃśatipati attained unwavering faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and he thought to himself:
"I shall don the armor of firm faith in order to attain the fruit of Buddhahood."
Then he spoke in verse:
"O devas, humans, and asuras!
This is the unsurpassed and most supreme understanding;
O Brahmā and the hosts of devas!
You do not see, nor can you know.
I shall, within this world, attain such a Dharma as this.
The wisdom of omniscience is certain and free from doubt.
In this world, you shall attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings;
you shall reveal and manifest the pure Dharma of the Buddha for countless koṭis.
The eight factors of the untainted liberation, the supreme and true path;
infinite wisdom fully revealed, endowed with the thirty-two marks.
Having attained Buddhahood and realized bodhi, he adorns his body therewith.
May all sentient beings universally be led to practice pure deeds;
may they transcend the stream of birth and death and extinguish all fears;
may they uphold the conduct of virtue and wisdom, providing rescue and vast benefit to others.
"The sun-body opens the moon-mouth; extinguishing dust, he shatters birth and death.
Upholding virtue, he shall become a Buddha and manifest within the three realms of existence.
At that time, after Vipaśyin had spoken these verses, he immediately [attained] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
Having attained non-retrogression in bodhi, they carry with them immeasurable and wondrous exotic objects according to their hearts' desires,
manifesting in various ways: diverse flower garlands, incense for burning, unguents, powdered incense, robes, banners, pennants, parasols,
clusters of maṇi jewels, silken canopies and curtains, and various ornaments such as necklaces of genuine pearls and gems.
Adorned with ornaments, they offered worship with the sounds of flutes, drums, and various songs and hymns;
their beautiful voices and pleasing melodies filled the void as they descended from the sky, led by their retinues like a king of geese approaching the Buddha’s presence,
and together before the Buddha, they knelt with their right knees touching the ground.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, performing several hundred bows. Having risen, he circumambulated the Buddha several thousand times to the right.
Then, before the Buddha, Vimaladatta threw himself upon the ground like a great tree falling, and spoke these words:

“Namo, namo to the Honored One whose body is adorned with boundless wondrous virtues; to the Supreme Man among men, the Lion, the Most Victorious Bhagavat of the three realms, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Having spoken thus, he rose and, with palms joined and a single-minded focus, praised the Buddha’s virtues in verse:
“Throughout immeasurable *koṭis* of births, You have accumulated and cultivated pure conduct;
Practicing deeds most difficult to perform, You have secured the cause for the attainment of Bodhi.”
Food, drink, clothing, and mounts; pearls, necklaces, gold, and the seven treasures—these he bestowed upon those who begged, in measureless hundreds of thousands of billions.
He abandoned his kingdoms, cities, and towns, as well as his loved ones and retinues.
The capital city of King Puṇyavanta was prosperous and joyful, with stores of wealth and treasures.
His will was courageous and free from narrowness; his saving deliverance was inconceivable.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, he constantly practiced the giving that is so difficult to relinquish.
In the past, when he was a prince named Sudāna,
He dwelt in a forest of asceticism and gave away his wife and children.
Once seeing a starving tigress with her cubs, Out of compassion, he sacrificed his own flesh and body.
Furthermore, to save the life of a dove, he did not begrudge having himself slaughtered and dismembered.
Seeing a blind Brahmin begging for his eyes, he immediately gouged them out and gave them;
never once did he give rise to suffering or distress, nor did he harbor any heart of regret.
Seeing those who come to beg, he gives with great joy and reverence;
for the sake of cultivating the causes of Bodhi, he sacrifices his head to the supplicant.
Throughout the long night, he guards the aggregate of precepts, remaining untainted and without flaw.
Pure, single-minded, and holy conduct, unmixed with any evil;
not harming the lives of sentient beings, nor stealing the wealth of others;
the Brahma-faring ever pure, untainted by stinginess or attachment.
Do not let false speech issue from the mouth; abstain from alcohol and all its varieties.
View all sentient beings with equanimity, as no different from oneself.
Never engage in divisive talk, nor sow slander to destroy others.
One does not utter violent speech, nor speak words that are frivolous or meaningless.
One constantly practices beneficial and wholesome conduct, restraining and eliminating all harm;
toward any sentient being, one does not give rise to even a moment of resentment or anger.
Constantly severing all false views, Dedicatedly upholding right and virtuous qualities;
In the places of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, Cultivating offerings with profound sincerity.
Having formerly renounced the five desires, Leaving home far from the stains of attachment;
I uphold the pure precepts of the Buddha, the Prātimokṣa.
In the past, I practiced the virtue of patience, calmly enduring all manner of suffering;
whether insulted, beaten, reviled, or cursed, I endured all such harshness and bitterness.
Never having a heart of resentment or regret, his mind never for a moment gave rise to evil;
toward all sentient beings, he was without harm, without disdain, and without anger.
With eyes of compassion he beheld all beings, regarding them universally as if they were his own children.
Causing them to be liberated from immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of great sufferings and poisons;
throughout life after life, they constantly practiced the path of great patience;
formerly they were the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, who cultivated the Way and expounded the pure Dharma.
The queen, palace ladies, and others came with joy to listen and receive [the teaching];
though the king’s anger sought to harm Great Patience, Great Patience’s mind remained peaceful and joyful.
The Holy Honored One established great diligence throughout inconceivable koṭis of eons.
The narrow, inferior, and indolent mind Is constantly restrained so that it does not arise.
With great resolve and vast diligence, One awakens to the Buddha’s Bodhi;
By means of the Buddha’s Great Bodhi, One brings all things to enlightened illumination.
In the past, you practiced difficult austerities, exerting yourself with diligence and without indolence;
you made offerings to all those worthy of honor and to immeasurable Tathāgatas.
Even for the sake of sentient beings, you remained within the cycle of birth and death.
Following along as a servant, he guided others through various skillful means;
throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, he performed great and arduous practices,
accumulating the cultivation of the Buddha’s true Dharma in order to pray for the unsurpassed fruit.
In the past, he cultivated meditative concentration, Tranquilizing and subduing the mind;
He fully attained the four dhyānas and the five supernormal powers, As well as the formless attainments and so forth.
Through right reflection, he perfected samādhi And the taintless concentrations.
In former times he cultivated Prajñā, fulfilling untainted wisdom;
He realized that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, being illusory, false, provisional, and deceptive;
There is no self and no sentient beings, No life-span, no nourisher, and no sustainer.
Beings revolve due to karma, their web of afflictions continuous;
the desire realm is ever impure, accompanied by the four types of defiled afflictions.
When the realm of sentient beings is purified, one then realizes the root of afflictions.
Having attained true purity, one sees the beginning of sentient beings.
Through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the transcendence of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth—
by what meaning are these revealed?
Through skillful means and the perfection of wisdom,
and by means of boundless, supreme accumulations of merit; through great diligence in the noble activities of body,
speech, and mind, the Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One, has now attained the true fruit of Buddhahood.
"I now prostrate in homage to the Great Father, the World’s Sole Reliance;
may I, in a future time, attain the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha.
At that time, the householder Vimala had finished praising the Buddha in verse.

With immeasurable varieties of exquisite flower garlands, burning incense, unguents, and powdered perfumes; with robes, parasols, banners, and pennants; and with flutes, drums, various musical instruments, songs, and hymns of praise.

He was held in the highest esteem by his followers, and together with them, he made offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas according to the Dharma and with sincere devotion.
At that time, Vipaśyin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask a few questions of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I pray that you will deign to grant me your permission.
The Buddha said to Vipaśyin:
"Ask whatever you desire; I shall explain it for you according to your mind."
Having received the Buddha’s permission, the householder Vimalaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding ‘sentient beings’ (*sattva*), which in the Brahma-sound is translated as ‘sentient beings’ or ‘sentient beings with emotion’ (*yuqing*): what is the meaning of this term?”
The Buddha said to the Lord of Laṅkā:

"Sentient beings are so called because they are a collection of various natures and perceptions. That is to say, earth, water, fire, wind, space, consciousness, name-and-form, the elements, the sense bases, dependent origination, and the fruits of causes and karma come together to arise, like a bundle of reeds; yet people grasp at them as a self."

Some say: "Sentient beings" refers to those who are born, those who are nurtured, or "great men" (puruṣa); they may be called *pudgala*, or *manava*, or "the knower," or "the seer," or "the doer," "the feeler," or "the perceiver."
"Lord of Laṅkā, you should know that all these are merely the conceptualizations of sentient beings.
Vīvidha then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
By what do those sentient beings take as their root?
Where do they dwell?
And by what are they carried along?
The Buddha said, "All sentient beings have ignorance as their root; they dwell in craving and are carried along by the flow of karma. Vimalā said:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of karma are there?
The Buddha said:
“Lord of Laṅkā! Karma is of three kinds and has three characteristics.
What are the three kinds?
That is to say:
bodily action, verbal action, and mental action.
What are their three characteristics?
That is to say:
the mark of the wholesome, the mark of the unwholesome, and the mark of both the wholesome and the unwholesome. Vīravikrāmin said:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that sentient beings, having died, undergo rebirth again?
How do they discard this body and take up a new body?”
The Buddha said: “Lord of Laṅkā!

When the bodies of sentient beings die and consciousness migrates, it is carried along by the winds of karma to undergo the fruits of their own actions—whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, or both wholesome and unwholesome.”

Drawn by the force of karma to receive the retribution of a body, one may undergo birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, or miraculous birth; in all cases, one arrives effortlessly, driven by the winds of karma.
Vivatsa said: “World-Honored One!
After sentient beings have died and received the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), but before they have received a new body, how do they abide?”
The Buddha said:
"Lord of Laṅkā, what do you think?"
Just as a seed produces a sprout, does the sprout arise after the seed has first perished?
Or does the sprout arise first and the seed perish afterward?
Or does the sprout arise only after a long time has passed since the seed’s destruction?
Viviṃcan said: “World-Honored One!

It is not that the sprout arises only after the seed has perished, nor that the seed perishes only after the sprout has arisen; arising and perishing are simultaneous, with neither prior nor posterior.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, Lord of Laṅkā!"

It is not that the final consciousness of the old body ceases and then the initial consciousness of the new body arises; nor is it that the initial consciousness of the new body arises and then the final consciousness of the old body ceases. Birth and cessation are simultaneous, with neither priority nor posteriority.
"Lord of Laṅkā!
It is like the movement of the *kīṭikā* insect: wherever its head goes, its entire body follows; once it has settled, it does not move until it takes another step.

In this same way, when the primary consciousness (*pūrva-vijñāna*) entrusts itself to a body, all other consciousnesses follow it; once entrusted, they do not depart until death brings about their transfer and relinquishment."
Viviṃśat said, "If this is so,
is there an intermediate state (antarābhava)?
The Buddha said:

"Lord of Laṅkā! Just as sentient beings born from eggs cast off their bodies and enter an egg, remaining within it as a congealed mass devoid of consciousness through the power of karmic winds, until the egg matures and consciousness finally awakens."
Why is this so? Such is the nature of karmic phenomena.
By the power of karma, egg-born sentient beings have no perception whatsoever until the time for their maturation has arrived.

Furthermore, when a Wheel-Turning King or a Wheel-Turning King’s son receives a body due to their meritorious karma, they are not defiled by the impurities of the womb; they are not mixed with such impurities, and because they are untainted by the womb's filth, they are mostly born through transformation.

Just as some who are born from a womb may possess both the womb and the egg yet remain unstained by the impurities of the womb, emerging after the time of maturation has arrived by splitting open the egg—
O Lord of Laṅkā, one should use this to illustrate the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Viviṃśat said: “World-Honored One,
what is the measure of consciousness?”
"What form and color does it take?
The Buddha said, "Lord of Laṅkā!"

“Consciousness is immeasurable; it is without color and without form, cannot be manifested, is unobstructed and without likeness, and has no abiding place nor any outward expression. Vimalaprabhā said:
“World-Honored One!”

If the substance of consciousness were limitless, formless, shapeless, and incapable of manifestation; if it were unimpeded, without resemblance, without abiding, and without expression—would this not be the characteristic of annihilation?
The Buddha said, “No, Lord of Laṅkā!”
I shall now employ a parable to illustrate your mind so that you may attain awakening.

It is as if you were within your own palace, situated upon a hall and throne, attended and surrounded by a retinue of court ladies and attendants; with couches, seats, and bedding arranged for your comfort and pleasure, and adorned with all manner of exquisite ornaments.

At that time, in the Great Garden of Aśoka, the shrubs and trees flourished and various flowers bloomed; whether by a gentle breeze blowing harmoniously or a violent wind raging fiercely, the fragrance of the Aśoka grove wafted into the palace.
"Lord of Laṅkā! What do you think?
Can the fragrance of that wind be smelled?"
Viviṃśat said: “World-Honored One!
Fragrance can be known by smelling.”
“Lord of Laṅkā! Can you also distinguish the fragrance of this particular flower? Vipaśyin replied:
"It can be known through discrimination. "Lord of Laṅkā!
Can one, by means of smelling, perceive the substance, the dimensions, the shape, and the color of the fragrance?"
Viviṃśat said: “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? The substance of fragrance has no manifest color, cannot be grasped, has nothing with which it can be compared, is non-manifesting, and has no fixed abode; how, then, could its dimensions, color, and so forth be perceived?
“Lord of Laṅkā! What do you think?
Is it because you cannot perceive the substance, measure, or color of a fragrance that this constitutes the characteristic of cessation?”
Viviṃśat said: “No, World-Honored One.”
"If it were a characteristic of being severed, how could it be known by smelling? "So it is,
so it is, Lord of Laṅkā!"
If the substance of consciousness were severed, there would be no characteristic of discerning birth and death. Lord of Laṅkā!
You should know that the substance of consciousness is supremely subtle and pure, yet it is defiled by adventitious stains—namely, ignorance, craving, habitual tendencies, karma, and so forth.
"Just as the realm of space is supremely pure, yet becomes defiled by the four pollutants of smoke,
clouds, dust, and mist; so too, Lord of Laṅkā,
is it with the nature of consciousness, which is pure, subtle, formless, immeasurable, and unimpeded, yet appears defiled by adventitious taints!"

Why is this? When observed through true wisdom, ultimately no sentient being can be found; there is no life-principle, no living being, no person, no pudgala, no knower, no seer, no thinker, no feeler, no doer, and no hearer, nor even form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and so forth.
Lord of Laṅkā!
Through the contemplation of true wisdom, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is found to be unattainable; they all arise through combination and possess no distinct nature.
Lord of Laṅkā!
One should train in this way so that sentient beings become steadfast and subtle, and do not wander into the desolate wilderness of birth and death.
What is meant by sentient beings being steadfast?
It refers to attaining and realizing *mahāyoga*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Those who are driven by karma have not yet perfected the Eightfold Path;
Only when one is liberated from karma and attains the outflow-free state does one bring benefit to the world."
Then, Vipaśyin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Within the realm of sentient beings, there are immeasurable and boundless numbers, like the sands of the Ganges, who have crossed over the vast and deep ocean of the three realms of existence—some crossing by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle, some by means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and others who have realized and attained unsurpassed Mahāyāna and become perfectly awakened Buddhas, in numbers that are limitless, inexhaustible, immeasurable, and incalculable.”

In the future it shall be the same: by means of the three vehicles, immeasurable and boundless beings—like the sands of the Ganges—will cross over and attain nirvana, yet the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.
“World-Honored One!
Seeing this matter, I do not know what to do, as if I have abandoned my work.
The Buddha said:
“Lord of Laṅkā! Do not neglect your duties. Why is that?
The realm of sentient beings has neither beginning nor end; the realm of empty space and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are likewise so.

Therefore, Lord of Laṅkā, you should know that the realm of sentient beings cannot be said to increase and cannot be said to decrease. Among these vast, deep-sea oceans of birth and death within the three realms of existence, immeasurable and boundless numbers of beings have already crossed over and are yet to cross over; yet the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases, just as the realm of empty space neither increases nor decreases, being without beginning, middle, or end.
Yet the realm of space is omnipresent throughout all things, unobstructed, effortless, unconditioned, and non-discriminative.
In this same way, Lord of Laṅkā!
whether at the beginning, the middle, or the end, the realm of sentient beings is entirely ungraspable.
If one attains realization and accords with the noble Dharma, then the realm of sentient beings is ultimately inexhaustible and never diminished, yet there are those who attain liberation.
Why is this? Because the nature of the realm of sentient beings is such that it is without beginning and without end.
Viviṃśat said: “World-Honored One!
What is this ocean of birth-and-death?”
The Buddha said: "Lord of Laṅkā!
The ocean of birth and death is like the great ocean."
Viviṃśat said, "What is the teaching of the Buddha, the Great Teacher?
The Buddha said:
“The Buddha’s teachings should be understood as being like a boat.
He asked again:
“What is a bhikṣu who has gone forth and possesses the Dharma?”
The Buddha said,
"A bhikṣu who possesses the Dharma is like a merchant traveling by ship.
He asked again:
“How does one uphold the instructions and precepts of the Great Teacher without deficiency?
The Buddha said:

“One who loves the Dharma, honors the Dharma, is contented, and guards the precepts; who follows the teachings of the Great Teacher and carefully maintains them without deficiency—just like a well-maintained ship, securely fastened and fully equipped with provisions, which a merchant boards, desiring to cross the great ocean.”
He asked again:
“What is a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)?
The Buddha said:
"A spiritual friend is like a boatman who steers a vessel.
He asked again:
"What is the power of the eightfold right path?"
The Buddha said:
"The eightfold noble path is like a ship that advances swiftly when held by the wind of right faith.
He asked again:
"What is the dhyāna-abhijñā-samādhi-samāpatti?
The Buddha said,
"The dhyāna-abhijñā-samādhi-samāpatti is like a jewel island."
He asked again:
"What are the seven factors of enlightenment?
The Buddha said:
“The seven factors of enlightenment are like the seven kinds of precious gems.
He asked again:
“As for those who attain the seven factors of enlightenment and realize the Mahāyāna, how is this so?”
The Buddha said:
"For example, it is like a merchant who takes the treasures of the seven clans and, satisfying his every desire, becomes a man of great wealth.
O Lord of Laṅkā!..."
Having attained the seven factors of enlightenment and realized the Mahāyāna, one practices the unsurpassed path and peacefully achieves Buddhahood; you should know that it is likewise so.
Excellent is the life of renunciation within the teaching of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The dense thickets of all suffering entangle sentient beings;
To rescue both oneself and others, One must sever those bonds of suffering.”
"Leaving the household life in the Buddha's teaching, one becomes a true son of the Tathāgata!
When sentient beings cultivate the Great Self with constancy, they accumulate practice until they become a refuge for the world.
At that time, Vipaśyin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"What is the analogy for these foolish people?

"It is like merchants whose ship is wrecked in the great ocean, and they die by drowning in the water."
"Lord of Laṅkā!

“World-Honored One!
If there are those who have broken the precepts and do not cultivate the holy life, yet maintain the appearance and deportment of pure brahmacarya;

The Buddha said, "Lord of Laṅkā! It is as if a merchant in the great ocean,

Those who obtain a broken plank reach the islands by means of the power of the wind;
those who obtain a corpse float out across the sea, for in the ocean it is the law that a corpse does not sink;
and as for those who cross by floating through the power of single-minded diligence and valor, they may be taken up onto the shore by the sea deities out of compassion, just as they had hoped.

Within my Dharma, there are those who have left the household life but broken the precepts, or who have broken the precepts and returned to secular life; yet they possess pure faith toward the Buddha and repent thoroughly;
or their minds are straightforward and pure;
or, although they have violated the precepts, they do not abandon a heart of compassion and vow for the happiness of all sentient beings.
Or they may receive the precepts again and maintain them with renewed vigor. Lord of Laṅkā!
For these reasons, even those who have gone forth in my Dharma and broken the precepts, or who have abandoned the precepts and returned to secular life, may still be reborn in the happy realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of births, One may accumulate various sinful karmas;
But by undergoing thorough repentance and renewing oneself, The sins are purified and shall no longer increase."
Vivṛddha addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are there?”
The Buddha said:
"Lord of Laṅkā! There are thirty-seven factors that assist the dharma of awakening."
That is to say:

the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; these are called the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
Vivatsa said: “World-Honored One!
How many gates to liberation are there?”
The Buddha said:
"There are three gates of liberation. They are as follows:"
"Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Vimalā asked: "How are these cultivated and perfected?"
The Buddha said:
"There are three ways in which cultivation is perfected. Namely:"
"Cultivation through detachment from defilement, cultivation through cessation, and cultivation through the transcendence of nirvāṇa. Vipaśyin asked:
"How many methods of treatment are there?"
The Buddha said:
"Briefly stated, there are three methods of treatment:

for those with excessive desire, one uses the contemplation of impurity; for those with excessive hatred, one uses the contemplation of loving-kindness; for those with excessive delusion, one uses the contemplation of dependent origination."
Viviṃśat said, "How many kinds of 'well-cultivated' are there?
The Buddha replied:
“There are four kinds of skillful cultivation:

namely, skillful cultivation of the aggregates (skandha), skillful cultivation of the elements (dhātu), skillful cultivation of the sense bases (āyatana), and skillful cultivation of the means (upāya).”
Viviṃśat said, “How does one observe? The Buddha said:
“Lord of Laṅkā! You should deeply contemplate dependent origination and the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths.

At that time, Vipaśyin circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, scattered flowers made of the seven precious gems over the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and experienced a joy and exultation such as he had never known before.
He asked in verse:
"What practice does the Bodhisattva perform, being so courageous and beneficial to the world?
Through generosity, ethical discipline, concentration, patience, and diligence, he sets out for supreme enlightenment."
"Seeking untainted, perfect wisdom, To transform and guide all sentient beings;
Becoming a Buddha, the most supreme field, Adorned with stainless jewels?
Having spoken this verse, the Buddha addressed Vipaśyin, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! Lord of Laṅkā!
Since you ask the Tathāgata about this matter, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!”
I shall explain it for you, Lord of Laṅkā!
A bodhisattva constantly practices in conjunction with the six pāramitās, and his mind is free from obstruction toward all sentient beings.
Lord of Laṅkā!

A bodhisattva who practices in this manner must not allow their progress to regress nor be defiled by worldly dharmas. They should further cultivate the superior practices of the Buddha-dharma, bring boundless sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and realize Mahāyāna, free from all obstacles to the Buddha-dharma.
Viviṃśati addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should I now practice so that I may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said, "Lord of Laṅkā! You should abandon the faults of pride and arrogance;

be without envy or stinginess; practice the four Brahma-vihāras; and with a mind intent on benefiting all sentient beings, refrain from killing, false speech, drinking alcohol, sexual misconduct, stealing, double-tongued speech, harsh words, and improper speech. Constantly and single-mindedly cultivate the mind of bodhicitta, the mind of the six pāramitās, the mind of benefiting sentient beings, and the mind of tranquil purity. Contemplate the manifold terrors of the various realms of existence, and deliver sentient beings from the suffering and afflictions of the three worlds."
Lord of Laṅkā!
If you now wish to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, you should understand it in this way:
"That which is called 'Buddha' is merely a provisional designation established by name."
Why is this? Lord of Laṅkā!
Because the Buddha-body is without essence, because the Buddha-body is without root, because the Buddha-body is without abiding, because the Buddha-body...
Because it is utterly pure; because the Buddha-body is free from dust; because the Buddha-body is without self; because the Buddha-body is without grasping;
because the Buddha-body is without form; because the Buddha-body is without marks; because the Buddha-body is without entry; because the Buddha-body is without exit;
because the Buddha-body is without weariness; because the Buddha-body is without limbs; the Buddha...
Because the essence of the Buddha is non-attached; because the essence of the Buddha is undefiled; because the essence of the Buddha is immeasurable;
because the essence of the Buddha is without an object of perception; because the essence of the Buddha is unmixed; because the essence of the Buddha transcends all spheres of entry;
because the essence of the Buddha is free from all conceptualization, false imagination, and speculative calculation; and because the essence of the Buddha transcends all realms of existence.
Because the Buddha-body is difficult to enter; because the Buddha-body is difficult to know; because the Buddha-body is profoundly deep;
because the Buddha-body is without letters; because the Buddha-body is without form; because the Buddha-body is fundamentally quiescent; because the Buddha-body is wondrously stainless;
because the Buddha-body is unsurpassed; because the Buddha-body is beyond analogy; because the Buddha-body is unattainable.
Therefore, because the essence of the Buddha cannot be severed, because the essence of the Buddha cannot be destroyed, because the essence of the Buddha cannot be differentiated,
because the essence of the Buddha is inconceivable, because the essence of the Buddha lacks intrinsic nature,

because the essence of the Buddha has no location, because the essence of the Buddha has no manifestation, because the essence of the Buddha is unimpeded, because the essence of the Buddha is without...
Because it is like [an illusion], because the Buddha-body is not subject to annihilation, because the Buddha-body is not subject to permanence, because the Buddha-body is equal to empty space,
because the Buddha-body is unequaled among equals, and because the Buddha-body is ineffable.
"Lord of Laṅkā! Such is the nature of the Buddha-body.
Those who seek the Buddha should seek the fruit of Buddhahood through non-seeking."
Why is this? One cannot realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the notion of a self-nature (*svabhāva*);

nor can one realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the notion of a self (*ātman*), the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*), the notion of a life-principle (*jīva*), the notion of a nourisher (*poṣa*), the notion of a person (*puruṣa*), the notion of an individual (*pudgala*), the notion of an agent (*kāraka*), the notion of an experiencer (*vedaka*), the notion of a knower (*jñātṛ*), the notion of a seer (*draṣṭṛ*), or the notion of a thinker (*mantṛ*).

Not giving rise to the notion of conditioned phenomena, not giving rise to attachment to dharmas, not giving rise to attachment to the aggregates, elements, and so forth, and even not giving rise to attachment to the Buddha—this bodhisattva is able to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this so? Lord of Laṅkā! Awakening (bodhi) cannot be taken as an object of cognition;
it cannot be grasped through its intrinsic nature, nor can it be realized through the grasping of permanence or annihilation.
Why is this? Lord of Laṅkā!
Because all phenomena inevitably return to destruction.
Vivṛddha said: "World-Honored One!
How should one understand all conditioned phenomena?"
The Buddha said, “Lord of Laṅkā!
All conditioned phenomena should be known and realized as being like an illusion, like a dream, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water, and like a city of the gandharvas.”

When this Dharma was being taught, the householder Vimalaprabha immediately attained the Bodhisattva samādhi called the Banner of Wisdom Light of the Unequaled Dharma Torch, as well as immeasurable samādhis and dhāraṇīs, such as the dhāraṇī of skill in all languages.
Having attained various samādhis and dhāraṇīs, Vimalaprabhā said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
I now thoroughly understand all conditioned phenomena."
The Buddha said: "Lord of Laṅkā!
How do you now thoroughly understand all conditioned phenomena?"

Viviṃśati said: "Like a dream, like an illusion, like an echo, like a mountain torrent, like the moon in water, like a great wind blowing through empty space, like autumn clouds, lightning, or a drop of water on a lotus leaf; like a bubble, like a lamp, like a city of the Gandharvas, like a rainbow, or like a mirage—I now understand that the intrinsic nature of all conditioned phenomena is entirely like this."

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head boundless rays of light in various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, silver, and purple—in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of varieties. Having radiated and illuminated countless Buddha-lands, he withdrew the luminous signs and drew them back into the crown of his head.
Then, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms and bowed; he then asked in verse:
"The One of Supreme Virtue, the Refuge of the World, does not manifest this boundless net of pure light without cause.
Who has awakened to supreme wisdom and received the Buddha’s prediction?"
“The Muni’s hundredfold net of light shines everywhere.
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:

“Do you see the lord of Laṅkā named Vīpāśa, who stands before me with palms joined, making great offerings to me, to the assembly of śrāvakas, and to the assembly of bodhisattvas, and by means of these roots of goodness, resolving his mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
“I have seen them, O Sugata!
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:

"This Lord of the city of Vimala-laṅkā, having made offerings to us—ten million billion hundred thousand Buddhas—and taking this root of virtue, shall cast off his body and be born by transformation in the world Padmôtpāda. There, the Buddha shall be named Padmaguṇaketudhvaja-svaravikrīḍita-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he will establish, maintain, and dwell in the teaching of the Dharma to transform and edify beings, and that world will be pure, with the Buddha’s lifespan being immeasurable."

Vivi will be born in that buddha-field and immediately attain the Bodhisattva stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), continuing until he attains the tenth Bodhisattva stage. After the passage of incalculable eons, he shall manifest in this Sahā world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named *Suvīramatigarjitasvarāgravibhūṣaṇasuvarṇatejo-vimalaprabhāketudhvajavijayaratnasaṃcayaguṇavyūhacūḍālaṃkāravikāsasujātanantābhivairocanavaiśvānarādhipati-rāja*. He shall appear in the world as one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader, a charioteer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, and a World-Honored One.
The world is named *Vidyutmaṇḍala* (Jewel-Lamp Garland).

Its ground is level and even, without elevations or depressions, hills or mounds, pits or chasms, gravel or stones, nor any impurities; furthermore, there are no women and no evil realms. The land is adorned and pure, and the multitude of bodhisattvas exceeds those in the world of the Tathāgata Anantaprabha.
The eon was named Illuminating Darkness.
That Buddha’s lifespan was immeasurable and boundless, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
"For this reason, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha smiles with a joyful countenance and manifests the sign of light from his crown.

At that time, Vipaśyin, having received from the Buddha the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, leaped for joy; his entire body trembled with solemnity as the bliss of the Dharma pervaded him, and he ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees.
In the midst of the void, he spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are empty and illusory, like a dream;
Their self-nature is non-existent, pure as space."
The "self" is non-self, and likewise lacks intrinsic nature;
I know it to be like an illusion, like a flash of lightning or a garland of flames.
There are the realms of birth and death, the aggregates, the life-force, and the lifespan.
In the beginning, the end, and the middle, there is not the slightest essence of any phenomenon.
Yet there is the ripening of karmic fruits and the realms of existence for sentient beings;
if one cultivates bodhi, pure wisdom will finally realize that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
When Vibiṣaṇa had spoken these verses, he descended from the air, circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, and sat down to receive his instruction.
At that time, within that great assembly as vast as the ocean, there were devas, nāgas, and asuras who attained realization of the Dharma;
and among the yakṣas and rākṣasas, there were those who gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Among the kiṃnaras and mahoragas, there are those who have attained unwavering faith in the Buddha-dharma;
among the garuḍas, gandharvas, and vidyādharas, there are all those who have attained samādhi, dhāraṇī, and realization of the Dharma, and have reached the stage of non-retrogression.

Thereupon, the earth shook violently and a wondrous light shone everywhere, such that even the dark places within this Buddha-world were all bathed in radiance. All evil realms and various sufferings were brought to rest. In the sky, the devas rained down flowers and beat drums; their songs and cries intermingled as they waved their garments in joy at encountering such a marvelous event.
At that time, Vīravīra, the rākṣasa lord, looked back at his own followers and addressed them all, saying:
"All of you should come together to the place where the Buddha is, and with respect and offerings, resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rākṣasas went together to where the Buddha was, joined their palms, bowed with bodies bent, and said to the Buddha:

“We now, before the Buddha, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; we give rise to the bodhicitta, set out upon the Mahāyāna, and receive and uphold the Mahāyāna.”
I vow that in the future, within this Sahā Buddha-field, I shall become a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who extinguishes unsurpassed sins and brings great benefit to all sentient beings.
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent!
Since you have now resolved to attain bodhicitta for the sake of seeking buddhahood, you should cultivate four dharmas.”
What are the four? First, do not allow the practice of your vows to become deficient;
second, always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Third, to offer sincere worship and provide for the Three Jewels at the three times each day;
fourth, not to delight in seeking the fruits of the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"If you all diligently cultivate these four dharmas, you will not be deluded or lose the bodhicitta.
At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed deeply with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

What roots of goodness did this Lord of the City of Vimala-laṅkā cultivate in the past, that he now performs such vast offerings, providing for the Tathāgata, the assembly of śrāvakas, and all the bodhisattvas; and having resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, he immediately receives a prediction of his attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieves non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?
The Buddha addressed the Naga King Sāgara:

"In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in this Sahā world named Mahākāruṇyotpādajñānadhvajaketu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, appearing in the world as one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader, a charioteer of men, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One; the world was also named Sahā."
The five turbidities of that land were just as they are today.
That Buddha taught and transformed sentient beings through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, and there were five hundred śrāvaka bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha was atop Mount Malaya, surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable devas, nāgas, and even non-human beings, as he preached the Dharma.

This Lord of Laṅkā, Vibiṣaṇa, was at that time a young rākṣasa also named Vibiṣaṇa, residing in the great city of Laṅkā. He was violent and powerful, with fierce teeth and a terrifying appearance; he had a broad belly and a small face, and was a nāga king who drank blood and ate flesh.
At that time, the young rākṣasa heard that the Buddha was on the summit of Mount Malaya and thought to himself:
"I cannot endure this; I shall now drive away that śramaṇa and his assembly of bhikṣus so that they leave this mountain and depart from my realm."
Why is this? If this śramaṇa remains on the peak of Mount Malaya, he will prevent me from catching and killing sentient beings in the great ocean, and I shall constantly suffer from hunger.
He then addressed the assembly of rākṣasas:

"You who possess great strength, valor, and prowess, you should all fully prepare your armor, clubs, bows and arrows, *laṅgala*, *tumara*, *trimuṇḍa* spears, long and short pikes and lances, *vajra*-cakra wheels, balls for throwing, battle-axes, and various other weapons of war. Quickly come to my presence; together with you, we shall pursue that śramaṇa and his followers, driving them out of my territory so that they may be forbidden from further disturbing our domain."

Thereupon, the young rākṣasa Vibiṣaṇa donned his armor and took up his weapons; accompanied by the rākṣasa host and all manner of martial equipment, he traveled through the air to the presence of the Tathāgata Mahākāruṇyajñānaketu. Halting in mid-air, he spoke to that Buddha on behalf of the rākṣasa host, saying:
"Begone, śramaṇa! Depart from this mountain peak and stay far away from my domain!"
“Do not be killed at night, you and your followers.

At that time, the Tathāgata Mahākāruṇyotpādajñānadhvaja manifested great supernormal powers; by the Buddha’s spiritual power, he caused all the rākṣasas to see themselves bound with fivefold fetters, surrounded and pressed upon from all sides by iron nets on ten faces, fleeing with no place to hide and unable to remain still.
The hosts of rākṣasas trembled with fear and were struck with terror, thinking to themselves: "Where shall we go now?
To whom shall we turn for refuge?"
"Who can provide protection?
At that time, in the assembly of that Buddha, there was a vidyādhara king named Ghanavyūha-guṇasañcaya-tejoraśmi, who had previously been a close friend of the young rākṣasa Vibiṣaṇa.
Then, the Vidyādhara said to the young boy: "O friend!

The Great Teacher of gods and humans, who is fully endowed with boundless qualities and dharmas, the most honored in the three realms and a treasure among sentient beings, the Buddha, the Bhagavān, who universally saves all through great compassion."

"You and your followers should quickly take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha of bhikṣus; by fully undertaking the three refuges and generating the bodhicitta, all your bonds will be naturally released."
When the vidyādhara ṛṣi had finished speaking these words, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, the young rākṣasa and his retinue joined their palms and with one voice proclaimed:
“Namo, namo to the Honored One whose body is adorned with boundless wondrous virtues, the Unsurpassed Great Compassionate Samyaksaṃbuddha!”

We now first take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha of Bhikṣus. Having taken these three refuges, we abide in the three refuges and resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When these words were spoken, the bonds upon the bodies of the young rākṣasa and the rākṣasa host were all completely loosened. They descended from the air to the place where the Buddha Great Compassion-Arising Wisdom Banner King was, circumambulated him three times to the right, and together prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Having offered their repentance and thanks to the Buddha, they returned together to their original abode.
“Nāga King! Do not harbor doubts.
This present Vīrūḍhaka, the Lord of the Yakṣas, was formerly the young rākṣasa named Vīrūḍhaka.
Those who constitute the retinue led by Vīrūḍhaka, the Lord of the Yakṣas, were formerly the host of rākṣasas belonging to that young rākṣasa.”

The youthful friend, the King of Vidyādharas who possesses the merit of profound meditative concentration and the majesty of accumulated radiance, is none other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitājñānābhijña.
When these words were spoken, the trichiliocosm shook violently, swaying and trembling like a boat upon the sea.
At that time, no sentient beings experienced fear or harm; all were peaceful and happy, and everyone practiced the ten wholesome paths of action.

In this great trichiliocosm, there are no Mount Mālyavat or Sumeru mountains, nor rivers, seas, cities, towns, villages, mountains, rivers, islands, mounds, precipices, Black Mountains, or wind-caves; nor are there gardens, groves, marshes, ponds, rivers, springs, or lakes. All elevations and depressions, rugged terrain, pits, and traps; all earth, stones, sand, and gravel; all insects, thorns, mud, and excrement—all such foul and impure things are completely cleansed away.

In this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold great thousands of worlds, the great radiance of Jambūnada gold shines everywhere, even reaching as far as the Iron Ring Mountains and all dark, hidden places; wherever it encounters them, it dispels the black darkness with its golden light. Because of this golden light, all other lights are eclipsed and the sun and moon do not appear. The suffering of all animals and those in the realms of ghosts is entirely stilled; gods and humans are peaceful and happy, free from all afflictions and miseries. The hungry receive exquisite food, the thirsty receive delicious drink, the naked receive clothing, and the poor receive heaps of jewels. The blind are able to see, the deaf are able to hear, the mute are able to speak, the sick are healed, the incomplete are made whole, and those bound in fetters or imprisoned are all set free.

At that time, all sentient beings were peaceful and happy; they were not oppressed by greed, hatred, or delusion. Free from envy and stinginess, they looked upon one another with hearts of loving-kindness, benefiting each other like fathers and mothers, elder and younger brothers, or elder and younger sisters. They were harmonious and joyful; the sounds of clamor and contention did not reach their ears, and all sorrow and fatigue came to rest.

The ground is as level as the palm of a hand and as translucent as lapis lazuli; it is adorned with various exquisite ornaments and is vast and magnificent. There are ponds made of the seven precious gems, filled with water possessing the eight qualities; their bottoms are strewn with golden sand, clear, bright, and pure. Within these ponds grow many exquisite lotuses, fresh, moist, and in full bloom, as large as chariot wheels—divine lotuses of the seven precious gems, possessing various colors and various fragrances, and whose touch is as soft and delicate as kācalindika cloth.

Supremely wonderful and delightful, extending for billions and hundreds of thousands of years, these were arrayed everywhere. Those precious lotus flowers were some one yojana in size, some two yojanas, some three, four, five, up to ten yojanas; twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, even as large as a hundred yojanas or a thousand great yojanas. These celestial jewel lotus flowers appeared in this Sahā Buddha-field, their fragrant moisture light and sprinkling, soft, supple, and comfortable. A gentle breeze blew over them, raining down various exquisite flowers—Māndārava, Mahāmāndārava, Mañjūṣaka, Mahāmañjūṣaka, Candra, Mahācandra, Prabhāsa, Mahāprabhāsa, and Viśuddha flowers—falling everywhere in abundance.

Fine powdered incense rained down from the sky, scattering everywhere; aloeswood, tagara, black aloeswood, gośīrṣa, and uragasāra sandalwood—clouds of their fragrant smoke flowed and pervaded this entire buddha-field.

Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of koṭis—beyond all measure and number—there arose supreme and wondrous kalpa-trees, formed of the seven precious gems, towering, vast, and perfectly rounded, covering everything; they hung with various kinds of precious garments and fabrics, were strung with multicolored silks and yak-tail whisks, and were adorned with exquisite networks of lamba-bells.

A rain of various seven-jewels—gold, silver, maṇi, pearl, vaidūrya, musāragalva, crystal, coral, agate, ruby, pearl necklaces, and various neck-ornaments, jade, and gems—fell in profusion, brilliant, radiant, and shimmering.
Furthermore, there fell a rain of various multicolored garments and silken fabrics from the heavens, such as those of the gods Kuvera, Śakra, and Kauśika.

Moreover, there fell Jambūnada gold, various jeweled inlays, and exquisite ornaments: crowns, head-dresses, flower-adornments, crest-jewels, throat-ornaments, half-necklaces, full necklaces, crescent-shaped earrings, armlets, rings, bracelets for the hands and feet, and *yaśana* tunics. All these fell as rain.
From the various *kalpavṛkṣa* trees and throughout the four directions for a hundred *yojanas*, and even up to a hundred thousand *yojanas*, [flowers] fell everywhere;
beneath each of these *kalpavṛkṣa* trees were hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite lion-thrones made of the seven precious gems, each throne being seven *puruṣa* in height.
Upon each of these thrones appeared a Bodhisattva seated, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks, magnificently adorned, and radiating brilliant light.

Before each of the bodhisattvas were ten million *koṭi-nayuta* wheels made of the seven precious gems. Upon each wheel sat a thousand celestial youths, performing various divine music whose five tones harmonized; they sang in chorus with skillful and alternating melodies that gladdened the heart and delighted the mind. With pure and sublime sounds, they recited these verses (*gāthā*):
“Peerless and equal to the peerless, The natureless self-nature;
The nature of all virtues, A marvel in the world.”
By cultivating the practice of precepts and so forth, one attains the most pure Dharma;
adorned with supreme excellence, it illuminates all worlds,
removing the many sufferings of the evil paths such as the hells.
Having eliminated defilement, anger, folly, and envy,
one attains purity; thus pure among humans,
the land becomes vast, level, and boundless.
There are no rivers, mountains, or seas; Mount Meru and Sumeru do not exist.
The ground is like the palm of a hand, pure as sapphire.
Forests of various colored jewels stand in rows, perfectly straight and aligned.
The assembly of bodhisattvas each sat upon jeweled thrones;
their golden radiance blazed so brightly that it eclipsed the sun and moon,
while countless jeweled ponds were filled with water possessing the eight virtues.
Jewel lotuses like wheels bloom in splendor within the ponds;
celestial palaces and jeweled halls shine brilliantly by the billions.
Multitudes of celestial youths sit together, performing wondrous celestial music.
The tones were exquisite, gladdening the ears and delighting the mind.
Through the Tathāgata’s supernormal power, the sounds of music proclaimed the Dharma.
Amidst these various musical sounds, there were expounded countless and immeasurable subtle and wondrous verses of the Dharma, such as gāthās.

At that time, among the assembly of devas and humans gathered before the Buddha, those who had set out for the Mahāyāna and were seeking the Mahāyāna all beheld such a buddha-field adorned with meritorious qualities and purified, as well as the boundless radiance of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers.
Those among the gods and humans who practice the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas neither see nor know the pure merit and adornments of the Buddha-field.

When the assembly of bodhisattvas beholds the Tathāgata’s supernormal power, radiance, and the majestic purity of the Buddha-field, they immediately attain immeasurable samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and unhindered liberations;
yet the great śrāvakas remain unaware and unknowing, all having entered the meditative absorption of cessation.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a peerless and perfectly endowed physical body and sat cross-legged upon a lion throne that was high, vast, and exactly one hundred *koṭi* yojanas in extent, upon which celestial jeweled robes had been spread.
Before the Buddha there appeared a lotus flower made of the seven precious gems, eighty-four koṭis of yojanas in height and breadth;
furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of lotuses, adorned and fully blossomed with soft, wondrous, and radiant light;
and there were established immeasurable and innumerable banners, pennants, parasols, and canopies, adorned with various exquisite and diverse jewels, far exceeding all calculation.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable pearl necklaces and silk ribbons strung with nets of various jeweled bells hanging down from the air.

Such vast and great supernatural powers and merit-adornments of the Tathāgata were immeasurable and innumerable, beyond words and beyond indication; these rare and marvelous phenomena, never before seen and never before heard, appeared within this buddha-field.
*The Scripture on Realizing the Seal of the Mahāyāna*, Scroll One;
*The Scripture on Realizing the Seal of the Mahāyāna*, Scroll Two. Also titled *The Scripture on Entering the Realm of Wisdom of All Buddhas: The Tathāgatagarbha of Vairocana*.
Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Divākara.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya had this thought: "For what cause and condition does the Buddha now manifest such great supernormal powers and unprecedented events to adorn the Buddha-field?"
"You should ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, to resolve what you do not understand.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt upon his right knee on the lotus flower, bowed with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“I have a doubt and wish to request your clarification; I pray that you will grant me your attention.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
“If you have a doubt, ask whatever you wish; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall eliminate it for you.”
Having received the Buddha’s permission, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause, for what condition, and on account of whom does this Sahā world manifest such a great, rare, and unprecedented phenomenon?”

The Tathāgata’s supernormal powers adorn all buddha-fields with merit, vast, exquisite, pure, and luminous; they eliminate all evils beyond description, such as have never been seen before and never heard of before.
“World-Honored One!
What matter is there such that all bodhisattvas, having witnessed this great supernormal power manifested in this world, are unable to comprehend it?
Thus did Maitreya Bodhisattva inquire in verse:
"How wondrous, Great Muni!
A marvel has appeared here: the earth trembles to the very limits of the ocean, and the world abides in purity.
Nets of golden light shine everywhere, universally extinguishing the darkness of the world."
Countless billions of precious lotuses, with precious trees adorned by myriad flowers;
koṭis of parasols, banners, and pennants, with pearl garlands and jeweled bells;
through the light of manifold merit and wisdom, may all evil realms be utterly eliminated?
“By what causes and conditions, O Holder of Virtue, is the Sahā buddha-field purified?
Having spoken this verse, the Buddha told Maitreya:
“You may sit again; unprecedented dharmas have appeared in this world, and I shall explain their causes and conditions for you.”

Maitreya! To the east, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in incalculable Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Victorious and Sublime Array of Pure Merit-Clusters Adorned with Jewels Producing Radiance. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Supreme and Subtle Blossoming Radiance Adorned with Supernormal Powers of the Dharma-realm Field, Single Canopy Manifestation Roaring Sound Sovereign Teaching Wisdom Vairocana-treasury Established Supernormal Power King. He currently resides there, maintaining, upholding, and abiding in the teaching of the Dharma to transform and edify sentient beings.
The world is pure and free from all evil realms; therein dwell the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten stages.

Among them is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitajñānābhijña, who has attained unimpeded mastery over all bodhisattva dhyānas, samādhis, samāpattis, abhijñās, and dhāraṇīs. Now, together with a palace adorned with various jewels and a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas beyond counting, he has come through the air to this Sahā buddha-field.
"Because of that noble being, these magnificent displays of supernatural power have appeared as a preliminary sign.

When the Buddha spoke these words, an immeasurable *koṭi* of light-nets from the Great Radiance Jewel Palace manifested in the sky, adorning it on all sides; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments and songs harmonized in concert, and various celestial flowers were scattered. A hundred billion *nayutas* of diverse, brilliant lights shone forth everywhere, reaching this Sahā world.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitajñānābhijña placed his palace of jewel adornment between the realm of desire and the realm of form; surrounded by his retinue, he descended from the air to the place where the Buddha was, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Having both performed their prostrations, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitājñānābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that out of compassion you will accept my jewel-adorned palace; may the Buddha sit within this palace and expound the peerless, profound, and wondrous Dharma for the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitājñānābhijña, saying: “Excellent,
excellent, O Noble One!”

"You have offered this palace adorned with jewels to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; you have successively made offerings of this palace adorned with jewels to Vipaśyin Buddha and the other Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, up to the thousand Buddhas, and now you offer it to me."
"Excellent, O Noble One!
Adorn the Sahā Buddha-field with this palace adorned with jewels.
At that time, Sāgara the Nāga King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Where is the Palace of Jewel Adornment now located, and what are its dimensions?
The Buddha told the Dragon King Sāgara:
“O Dragon King, the Palace of Jewel Adornment now dwells in the space between the desire realm and the form realm; its dimensions are equal to those of a trichiliocosm.”
That Palace of Jewel Adornments is produced by the power of the supernormal knowledges and samādhis of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
it is a place where all Bodhisattvas sport in the Dharma and joyfully make offerings to the Tathāgatas.

The Buddha’s movements and abidings are perfected through his roots of goodness; he purifies the bodhisattva mind, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions, and fulfills the hearts of immeasurable sentient beings with joy. Surpassing all the palaces of the devas, bodhisattvas from the ten directions have all assembled there, where boundless and supreme forms provide a subtle and wondrous adornment throughout.

“Nāga King! In the Palace of Jewel Adornment, the ground is made of white lapis lazuli, the walls are of Jambūnada gold, and the balustrades are made of the treasure of supreme store. All the gate-towers and pavilions are of agate and the treasure of maṇi-store, with the jewel of stainless light serving as the railings, and the universally radiant exquisite jewel serving for the terraces, halls, and so forth.”

It was covered with crescents of all manner of exquisite jewels; the boundless, long world-systems were radiant and magnificent in number, eighty of them planted within jeweled palaces. Adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of ornaments, their brilliant light manifested clearly, with various wonderful jewels interspersed as decorations around them—all of which were supreme realms appropriate for the Tathāgata.

Hanging from them were various necklaces and trees of many banners and victory standards; suspended there were immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) exquisite and beautiful pennants and parasols. Silk streamers were threaded through nets of bells, and *nāga-uragasāra* sandalwood was ground to smear the ground. Incense such as aloeswood (*agaru*) and other sublime fragrances were burned, while *nāga-jewel*, precious flowers, and various celestial blossoms were strewn about as offerings.

Upon the crests of all the banners, thousands of koṭis of celestial youths sit and perform various musical instruments; the five notes blend harmoniously in alternating sequences, their exquisite, clear, and resonant tones gladdening the heart and delighting the ear, flowing everywhere throughout the world so that all beings find perfect joy.

“Dragon King! Above the accumulated winds, in the Palace of Jewel Adornment, there are thousands of koṭis of ponds made of the seven precious substances, their bottoms strewn with golden sand. They are clear, bright, and pure, filled with the eight qualities of water. Countless koṭi-nayuta hundreds of thousands of exquisite, multicolored lotuses made of the seven precious substances radiate brilliant light; they bloom wide and expansive like chariot wheels. Jewel groves are distributed all around, with kalpa-trees standing in rows, and various jewel flowers, various nets of bells, pearl necklaces, garlands, silk streamers, garments, and kara-pa ornaments provide subtle and wonderful adornments.”

Various fragrant incenses wafted through the air as jeweled terraces stood in alternating array; their radiance intermingled and reflected one another in a brilliant and dazzling splendor. Beneath each of the various jeweled trees was a high, broad, and most exquisite lion throne, fully adorned and draped with celestial, wondrous garments hanging down on all sides—seats fit for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to occupy.
All the exquisite, beautiful, and magnificent adornments of the worlds in the ten directions, as well as rains of incense, flowers, and jewels, all appeared within this precious palace.
“O Dragon King!
You should know that the location and the dimensions of the Palace of Jewel Adornment are exactly as such!
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of Bodhisattvas, including Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitājñānābhijña:
"O noble beings!

All of you should ascend with me to this precious palace. Seated within this precious palace, I shall fulfill the aspirations of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitājñānābhijña."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and, surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas beyond calculation, whom he honored and revered as they attended him before and behind, proceeded through the air with a composed and serene manner. To his right stood the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati-gambhīra-vikrīḍita-jñānābhijña, and to his left stood the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
The Buddha, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, ascended to the center of the precious palace and sat facing east upon a lion throne that was immeasurable *yojana*s in height and breadth.

When the Buddha ascended the lion throne, the Palace of Precious Adornments shook in six ways, and from the palace issued forth nets of great radiance in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, silver, purple, and crystal.

The youths of the devas beat drums, blow horns, sing songs, and perform various musical ensembles; they rain down great celestial flowers and burn exquisite divine incense, which waft in fragrant profusion, scattering and drifting down in abundance.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Each of you should sit upon the lotus flowers that have been prepared for you.
Then, the bodhisattvas, receiving the Buddha's instruction, sat down.

When the assembly had all taken their seats, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati-gambhīra-vikrīḍita-jñāna-abhijña stood foremost before the Buddha together with the host of bodhisattvas and thought to himself:
"We should now make offerings to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and inquire about the stages of a buddha."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravicāraṇajñānābhijña rose from his seat and, according to his intention, created the most supreme, excellent, and wondrous offerings—beyond the reach of ordinary beings—consisting of immeasurable and boundless varieties of flower garlands, incense for burning, unguents, and powdered incense; robes, banners, pennants, and parasols; as well as the sounding of drums, flutes, singing, and the harmonious emergence of various musical tones and Brahma-like hymns of praise. Together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, he paid homage with reverence and respect, making extraordinary and sincere offerings to the Buddha and the bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, he again performed supreme offerings to worship the Buddha. With necklaces of precious jewels, *nāga-śrī* sandalwood, seven-jeweled flower stamens, the *Amogha-ratna-nidhi*, and pure, radiant great *maṇi* gems, he scattered them over the Tathāgata. He then spread them out and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the World-Honored One hundreds of thousands of times, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke in verse:
“Your body is adorned with the most excellent and wondrous marks, Perfectly complete and peerless in its majesty;
The hair on your crown is pure, dark blue, and curls to the right, Radiant like a peacock’s plumage or a black bee.”
The forehead is broad, level, smooth, radiant, and clear; the tip of the ūrṇā-kośa is brilliantly white, opening with lush beauty.
The two eyebrows are curved like the crescent moon; the mark of the nose is upright and majestic, beyond compare.
His eyes are like freshly opened petals of the blue lotus; his ears hang down with supple luster like the stalks of the banana tree;
his superior teeth are brilliant, white, even, and closely set, as radiant as blossoms newly blooming in full bloom.
The tongue is broad, thin, and radiant with the luster of red copper; it obtains the most excellent flavor among all flavors.
The face is like the full moon, shining with brilliant clarity; the vermilion lips are the color of the bimba fruit.
The cheeks and jaws are full, robust, and prominent; the exquisite arms hang long like śāla trees.
The webbed fingers are as fine and beautiful as those of a king of geese, and the superior nails possess a luster like red copper.
The palms bear the auspicious marks of exquisite wheels; through billions of accumulated births, he has extensively bestowed virtue.
The front portion of the Muni is like that of a lion, his neck adorned with beautiful and supreme marks.
The waist has the mark of a vajra, and the abdomen is concealed; the lower body is secret, its features hidden and not manifest.
The thighs and shanks are straight like an elephant’s trunk, with webbed fingers like a goose’s and exquisite, beautiful ankles.
Your feet are level and upright, adorned with wheels; the Holy Honored One walks with the gait of a lion.
Possessing all the supreme marks, you have attained perfect enlightenment; I now prostrate before the Honored One of virtuous marks.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitājñānābhijña, having praised the Buddha in verse, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask something; I only pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha will deign to show compassion and grant me permission.
The Buddha said, "Noble son!"
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it to you according to your questions, so as to bring you understanding.
Having received the Buddha’s permission, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitājñānābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How many stages of the Tathāgata are there that all bodhisattvas cannot traverse, and which are not within the realm of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?
The Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Sāgaravaradharagambhīravikrīḍitājñānābhijña, saying: "Excellent, excellent!"
"O Noble Being!
Your inquiry into this meaning before the Tathāgata will universally bestow great radiance upon all bodhisattvas, opening the Buddha’s true wisdom and bringing about great benefit and great peace."
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall speak for you. "O Noble One!"
There are ten stages of the Tathāgata.
Even all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are unable to practice them, let alone the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas!
As for the ten stages of the Tathāgata, the first is named the Stage of the Wisdom of the Most Victorious, Profoundly Deep, and Difficult-to-Perceive Vimala Radiance.
The second stage is called the Ground of Inconceivable Radiance that Adorns the Body with Stainless Majesty;
the third stage is called the Ground of the Ocean-Treasury of the Jewel Banner of the Moon of Wondrous Radiance.
